Parsing command-line arguments with argitect

Zuguang Gu (guzuguang@suat-sz.edu.cn)

2026-11-24

argitect.Rmd
## Warning: package 'knitr' was built under R version 4.6.1

argitect (a phonetic approximation of “arkitect”) is a pure-R command-line argument parser. It reimplements the functionality of the Perl module Getopt::Long without any external dependency, and additionally supports positional arguments and flexible help messages.

A quick example

The following code is normally put to the beginning of an R script:

library(argitect)

cutoff = 0.05
argitect(
    "number=i", "Number of items.",
    "cutoff=f", "Cutoff for filtering results.",
    "verbose!", "Print messages."
)

The script (if the script is called foo.R) is then executed with command-line arguments, for example in one of the following forms:

~\> Rscript foo.R --number 4 --cutoff 0.01 --verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R --number=4 -cutoff=0.01 --verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R -n 4 -c 0.01 -v
~\> Rscript foo.R -n4 -c=0.01 -v
~\> Rscript foo.R -n=4 --no-verbose

In this example, number is a mandatory option and it should only be in integer mode. cutoff is optional and it already has a default value 0.05. verbose is a logical option. If parsing is successful, two variables number and verbose will be imported into the working environment with the specified values. Value for cutoff will be updated if it is specified in command-line.

The help message is automatically generated according to the option specification.

~\> Rscript foo.R --help
Usage: Rscript foo.R [options]

Options:
  --number, -n integer
    Number of items. 
  --cutoff, -c numeric
    Cutoff for filtering results.
    [default: 0.05] 
  --verbose, --no-verbose
    Print messages.
    [default: off] 
  --help, -h
    Print help message and exit. 
  --version
    Print version information and exit.

Specifications

Each specifier of command-line options consists of two parts: the name specification and the option specification.

length|size|l=i@{}

Here length|size|l is a list of option names separated by |, where length is the main option name, and others are aliases. The remaining part (i@{}) is the option specification which defines the data mode, the storage structure, and the range of arguments.

[option name|alias name...]=[mode][structure][constraint]

The option name

In a specification, there is a main option name. Multiple alias names are allowed. The main argument name must only contain letters, numbers, two characters of _ and .. It must be a valid R object name. There is no naming restriction for alias names. In the following example:

length|size=i

It can be specified as one of

~\> Rscript foo.R --length 12
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 12

both pointing to the length option. When partial matching from the first character is unique, users can provide a part of the option name.

~\> Rscript foo.R --len 12
~\> Rscript foo.R --si 12

It does not matter whether the command-line argument is specified by -- or -, or the value is specified by a space or =.

~\> Rscript foo.R --length=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -length=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -len=12
~\> Rscript foo.R --size=12

If the first letter of the option name is unique, it can be used as a single-letter flag.

~\> Rscript foo.R -l 12
~\> Rscript foo.R -l=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -l12

Since the main argument name does not allow the character of "-", for multi-word option, underline can be used to connect words while in the command-line interface, hyphen can be used.

min_length_of_word=i

then under command-line, this option can be set via (of cource --min_length_of_word 10 also works):

~\> Rscript foo.R --min-length-of-word 10

Data modee

Four data modes are supported, which are logical, integer, numeric and character, encoded by a single-letter:

  • l, logical
  • i, integer
  • f, numeric
  • s, character

For example, verbose=l is the same as verbose!. The configuration of logical options will be introduced in Section Logical argument.

Particularly, for the integer mode, besides providing a normal decimal integer under the command-line, integers in the binary, octal, and hexadecimal forms.

num=i
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 20
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0b10100
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0o24
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0x14

Where do the options go

Options will be imported into an environment as R variables. By default it is the environment where argitect() is called. The first name in option name specification is taken as the corresponding variable name. That is why we require the first name to be a valid R object. If the R variable is already defined with proper value, the corresponding option will have default value, and is then called an optional option that not mandatory to be specified on the command-line.

cutoff = 0.05
argitect(
    "number=i", "Number of items.",
    "cutoff=f", "Cutoff for filtering results.",
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)

print(number)
print(cutoff)
print(verbose)

In this example, cutoff already has a default value 0.05, thus it is optional on the command-line.

~\> Rscript foo.R --number 2 --verbose
[1] 2
[1] 0.05
[1] TRUE

Note the format of the default value of an option should be compatible to the corresponding specification. We will introduce it in later sections.

Logical argument

A logical option always has a default value of FALSE if it is not created in advance.

argitect(
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)
Usage: Rscript foo.R [options]

Options:
  --verbose, --no-verbose
    Print message.
    [default: off] 
  --help, -h
    Print help message and exit. 
  --version
    Print version information and exit.

"verbose!" and "verbose=l" are identical. A default value can also be set for logical option.

verbose = TRUE
argitect(
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)
Usage: Rscript foo.R [options]

Options:
  --verbose, --no-verbose
    Print message.
    [default: on] 
  --help, -h
    Print help message and exit. 
  --version
    Print version information and exit.

The negation of a logical option can be specified as one of:

~\> Rscript foo.R --no-verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R --not-verbose

If a single letter flag is available for each logical option, they can be bundled to call.

argitect(
    "close!",  "Close the connection.",
    "delete!", "Delete the file.",
    "exit!",   "Exit the script."
)
Usage: Rscript foo.R [options]

Options:
  --close, -c, --no-close
    Close the connection.
    [default: off] 
  --delete, -d, --no-delete
    Delete the file.
    [default: off] 
  --exit, -e, --no-exit
    Exit the script.
    [default: off] 
  --help, -h
    Print help message and exit. 
  --version, -v
    Print version information and exit. 
~\> Rscript foo.R -cde
~\> Rscript foo.R -cd -e

Or manually set a single-letter name for each logical option:

argitect(
    "close |a!",  "Close the connection.",
    "delete|b!",  "Delete the file.",
    "exit  |c!",  "Exit the script."
)
Usage: Rscript foo.R [options]

Options:
  --close, -a, --no-close
    Close the connection.
    [default: off] 
  --delete, -b, -d, --no-delete
    Delete the file.
    [default: off] 
  --exit, -c, -e, --no-exit
    Exit the script.
    [default: off] 
  --help, -h
    Print help message and exit. 
  --version, -v
    Print version information and exit. 
~\> Rscript foo.R -abc

Data structures of options

There are three structure of option values: a single element, a vector-like object and an object of name-value pairs. Each structure has a special mark symbol represented.

Scalar

The symbol for the scalar data structure is $, however, it can be ommited because it is the default symbol if not specified.

size=i$
size=i

Logical options also correspond to logical scalars, their specification is one of:

verbose=l
verbose!

A bare symbol of positinoal argument also returns a scalar.

pos=i#

If an option has a default value, the data mode and structure should be compatible with the corresponding specification.

Vector

Technically, in R, a scalar is a vector of length 1. However, here we discriminate these two scenarions. The symbol for vector/array is @, where a list of values can be specified after the option name.

argitect(
    "size=i@", "size"
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3

A positional option explicitely with {} also accepts a list of values.

argitect(
    "rgb=i#{}", "RGB channels."
)
~\> Rscript foo.R 255 10 10

Hash

It is not proper to call it a hash since the option is stored as a list while not a hash. However, the argitect package is developed based on the Perl module Getopt:Long where % stands for hash. So here we still call it a hash to emphasize it contains name-value pairs.

The symbol for vector/array is @, where a list of name-value pairs are specified after the option name.

argitect(
    "size=i%", "size"
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size a=1 b=2 c=3

Option constraint

For the options in the structure of vector and hash, the amount of elements can be further controlled.

argitect(
    "size=i@{2,3}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3
argitect(
    "size=i@{,3}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 
argitect(
    "size=i@{3,}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 4

A set of names can be set in {} then the option will be a named vector. In the next example, size can only accept two elements.

argitect(
    "size=i@{foo,bar}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2

Adding a tailing comma allows more self-defined names besides those having been provided.

argitect(
    "size=i@{foo,bar,}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2 abs=3 xyz=4

Similar for hash, the following example only allows two elements for size. The command-line usages is the same, but here size has the value of list(foo = , bar = ), while in previous vector-based example, size has the value of c(foo = , bar = ).

argitect(
    "size=i%{foo,bar}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2
argitect(
    "size=i%{foo,bar,}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2 abs=3 xyz=4

Being different from vectors, elements in a hash (or a list) can in different modes. The the data mode can be defined as i% which globally controls the data mode of all its elements. Also data mode can be set for individual elements.

In the next example, the global mode is integer i, sub-argument foo has its own mode f and bar inherits the global one.

argitect(
    "size=i%{foo=f,bar}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1.5 bar=2

If the data mode is not specified on the global level, then every individual sub-option should explicitely specify its data mode.

argitect(
    "size=%{foo=f,bar=i}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1.5 bar=2

Besides sub-argument as scalars, they can also be vectors. In the next example, sub-argument foo expects a list of integers. For the list of values assign to a sub-argument, elements should be separated by one of ",", ";", ":", "|" and "/" without spaces.

argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i@,bar=f}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1,2,3,4 bar=1.5

Similarly, constraints of sub-argument can be set as follows.

argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i@{2,3},bar=s@{1,2}}", ""
)

For positional options, one or two numbers can be used to specify the ranges of the number of values.

argitect(
    "size=i#{3}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3

In the option specification, names are also allowed.

argitect(
    "rgb=i#{red, green, blue}", ""
)
~\> Rscript foo.R 255 128 128

In above example, rgb is stored as c(red = 255L, green = 128L, blue = 128L).

Note positional option does not allow tailing comma.

Positional options

Positional options can be put as the first few options or the last few options in the specifications.

argitect(
    "size=i", "Size.",
    "cutoff=c", "Cutoff.",
    "file=s#", "File"
)
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 10 --cutoff 0.01 input.txt

Or

argitect(
    "file=s#", "File"，
    "size=i", "Size.",
    "cutoff=c", "Cutoff."
)
~\> Rscript foo.R input.txt --size 10 --cutoff 0.01
